title: The northern lasse a comoedie. As it hath beene often acted with good applause, at the Globe, and Black-Fryers. By his Maiesties Servants. VVritten by Richard Brome.
author: Brome, Richard, d. 1652?

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
BVt I beseech you sir, Take me somewhat
nearer your Councell. May I assure my
selfe, that this report goes true; that you
are on this treaty of Marriage with that
Widow?

speeches.speaker: Luc
prose:
Faith cosen, I take it as my fortune; and ^m fully
bent on the aduenture.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
Troth in my mind, you were better venture your
selfe, and fortune to the Bermudas. Tis true, shee has a
good estate: some nine thousand, I thinke: and were an apt
match for one that knew how to governe it, and her; some
hard bred Cittizen, crafty Lawyer, or countrey Iustice. But
you, a tender Nur^eling of the Court, altogether vnmixt
with such nature or education, to cast your selfe vpon her,
who for her yeares might be your Mother (they say: I never
saw her) and has beene the Towne widow these three
yeares, still conversant with Doctors, and Proctors of the
civill Law; of which Tribe her husband was too. Never
looke to bee the better for her Riches: Shee'll consume
yours and you too. though your backe were Herculean; and
lay you in your graue, or in Bedlem (my life on't) before she
dreame o' dying, though it be all that you can hope, or pray
for, after Mariage.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose:
You speake sir out of some vnfortunate examples,
and your extraordinary care of me. But truth is, all deswasion
comes too late; and all vrgings against it are now vncharitable:
For wee are already Man and Wife.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: What married!

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Lustily promis'd sir. Absolutely contracted.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: Send you ioy. Ile out of Towne.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose:
I hope you'll see our Mariage. I sent indeed to bid
you.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
No, good sir Phillip, rather then I would be in sound
of a Bell that should ring at it, I would haue my braines fillipt
out with the Clapper.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose:
Nay good cosen: I intended you my principall
Guest. Wee'll haue all very priuate: not aboue foure or fiue
friends more.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
Sir, I intend to bee none of your Mourners, which
indeed my presence there would m^ke mee; and so, perhaps,
infect the rest. I leaue my best wishes to you, and will indeauour
to pray for you. Indeed I will.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Indeed this is very abrupt.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose:
Mr. Tridewall! well met. Why so fast sir, I tooke
you for a Foot-post.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
A Foot-post! Indeed your fine wit will post you into
another world one of these dayes, if it take not the whipping
post i' the way. And why Foot-post, in your little witty
apprehension?

speeches.speaker: An.
prose:
Because you went so fast. B^t since you are angry,
I would you were going twise as last. If I interrupt you,
hang me. Dee heare?

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
Nay I know you are apt to decline any mans anger,
good Captaine Anvile: you haue beene beaten to't.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
Why, if he haue, hee may thanke such as you are,
that can endure no iest.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: What are you there too? Mr. Widgine, I take it?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
My name is Walter Widgine sir, not to be denyed. the
only brother here of sir Phillip Lucklesse his betroch'd. She
is a Widgine borne sir, and of the best family: Our Ancestors
flew out of Holland in Lincolnshire to preuent peri^cation.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
From Crowland, I warrant you, a little before a
Moulting time.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
Like enough sir. My sister can tell you. Since, by marriage,
shee was made a Fitchow: Her husband was Fitchow
the civill Lawyer; Hee was call'd the great Canno^r of
the civill Law: because he could dischardge or make report
of euery Canon therein; Canon after Canon, or Canon vpon
Canon at his fingers ends, as readily as I can tell these
peeces.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: A faire Demonstration!

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
He had many rare parts in him, besides sir, as my
sister can tell you.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
This fellow cannot chuse but haue a rare sister: Hee
quotes her so!

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
But all the good I can speake of him is, that he left
my sister rich; or at least a reasonable estate, halfe a score
thousand pounds or so: which shee, with her selfe, bestowes
vpon this honourable knight sir Phillip Luckles, to bee a Lady.
of that name, and God gi' him ioy. And for you: being
his kinsman, I shall desire your neerer acquaintance.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: In good time sir.

speeches.speaker: VVid.
prose:
The match was not altogether her owne seeking
sir, though she refus'd two Aldermen for him, on my owne
knowledge.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: Might shee haue had'hem both sir?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
I and halfe a score Aldermens fellowes to boote: yet
refus'd all for him.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
In deed sixe yoake of such cattell would plow vp all
his acres in a forenoone.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: My sister can tell you more sir.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
Still shee is his Authority. I will see this woman.
Sir Phillip, here are Guests will applaud your match. Bid'hem
welcome. God buy.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
For my part I honour any Man, that marries my



sister. Sir Phillip, and my noble brother in expectation, I
pray embrace my Governour, Captaine Anvile, here; and
giue him and me our gloues: you shall find him worthy your
acquaintance. Hee has wit, I can tell you; and breakes as
many good iests as all the VVits, Fits, and Fancies about the
Towne, and has traind vp many young gentlemen, both
here, and in diuers parts beyond the Seas. Hee was dry nurse
(thats one of his owne iests vpon himselfe) to the English
youth, a dozen yeares together beyond Sea: And now he is
my Governour, and I find profit in it: you cannot thinke
what an asse I was before I met with him: And I meane to
trauell with him, two or three yeares hence, my selfe. In
the meane time, he shall spend a hundred a yeare out of Wat
Widgines purse. Sha't ^faith Governour, what aylest thou?
art thou not right?

speeches.speaker: Anv.
prose: I shall find a time to right my selfe, I doubt not.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: But will you trauell at these yeares Mr Widgine?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
Will you not call me brother? Two dayes hence
when you haue married my sister, you must. Must hee not,
Governour?

speeches.speaker: Anv.
prose: Yes an't please him.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Hee ayles something.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose:
VVell then, Brother two dayes hence, will you
trauell?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
I some two yeares hence, mistake me not. I know
I am but young yet: besides I meane to marry first as other
young heires doe. And then towry lowry, faith, my noble
Governour, and I! Twill be braue going into France then: I
may learne halfe their fashions before I goe, and bate so
much, being taught at when I come there. VVhats the matter
Governour? thou wert not wont to bee thus. Is thy
money all gone? Heres fiue peeces to buy pomps against
my sisters wedding.

speeches.speaker: Anv.
prose:
Haue I eyes and eares, and can thinke of trifling
Money matters?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
Pox on't I had forgot. That sciruy surly gentleman
angerd him ere while, and put him out of patience. How the
hot ^ome of his rage boyles out at his Mouth. If I durst



goe so neere the heate of him I would skim the pot.

speeches.speaker: Anv.
prose:
If I try not this Tridewell; put him to the dearest
tryall of his life.—

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
I there tis, he will never come to himselfe till he beat,
or bee beaten.

speeches.speaker: Anv.
prose:
Let me haue these knockd out; these puld off; these
pluckd out, and these sawd off.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
I must venter on him. Nay Governour: pray thee
consider.—

speeches.speaker: Anv.
prose:
The time and place you meane. Thinke you hee
durst haue done it, but in his kinsmans house; hee and the
multitude of his seruants present.

speeches.speaker: VVid.
prose:
I, and wee know not how many arm'd men in the
next roome. Hearke Governour.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose:
What things are these! I shall marry into a fine
stocke! How vntimely some considerations fall into my
mind. My Cosens councell, which hath ever beene oraculously
good; against which I violently beare my selfe, to
mixe my blood amongst a race of fooles. Had but these
thoughts beene mine but one day past, they had preuented
all that may proue dangerous in this, so great and doubtfull
vndertaking.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: Sir, there's a gentlewoman would speake with you.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Who is it? Doe you not know her?

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose:
I never saw her before sir. I askt her name. But I perceiu'd
some displeasure in her looke (whether it were shame,
grie^e, or anger I know not) that made her conceale it: Only
telling me shee was a woman very hurtlesse, and warrantable
against your feare.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
I warrant tis my sister. Shee frownd, did shee not,
and look'd fightingly? If shee did, 'tis my sister, your wife
that shall be. Shee will looke so at you, I can tell you, or me,
or my Governour, for all he is a Captaine. Shee feares no
colours I faith, to tell you true, shee beate him once for a



iest he broke vpon her Monkey. Is it not shee, thinkst thou?

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: No sir it is not shee. I know my Lady that shall be.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
My Lady that shall bee! how sweetly it chimes.
Heres something for that word.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose:
Goe bring her vp. Good brother VVidgine, fly into
the next roome, with your Governour. Ile waite on you
presently.

speeches.speaker: VVid.
prose:
My Lady! And brother VVidgine! I must admire.
Our house is rays'd by this two stories higher.—

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose:
There's no recalling time; and vowes of this high
nature are no trif^les.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Sir I suppose you are sir Phillip Luckles.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I am the man Lady.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:
And you are shortly to marry a Citty Widdow, one
Mistresse Fitchow?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Most true.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:
For whose deare sake you purchas'd a foure hundred
pounds knighthood, to goe a woing in: out of which
shee is to giue nine thousand pounds for a Ladiship for terme
of life.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: What meane you Gentlewoman?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:
Sir not to scold, or brawle, (a vice to frequent in our
Sexe.) But, in few words (and ciuill ones) to make you sensible
of a little of that infinite iniury, you haue done to one,
whose vnvaluable portion of vertue makes her fit, (besides
the right shee has already in you) to take a brides place, before
your later choy^, or any shee, whose wealth might
weigh downe hers. You stand as if you knew not who I
meane.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Nor what neither. Sure my name's abus'd.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:
Pray sir bethinke your selfe. Has there not beene a
former contract made betwixt you and some other.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: No. Nor any faithfull promise neither.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: That I may well beleeue, when you forget it.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose:
I pray speake nearer to my vnderstanding: whom
may you suggest to be the woman ^o much forgotten?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
verse: If pitty, loue, or thought of me,
Liue in your breast I need not die.
But if all these from thence be fled;
Liue you to know, that I am dead.
prose:
If you haue soule, or sense, you must remember her:
No? Read then her name subscrib'd to that.

Farewell good Constance. I am sorry I haue no further
for thee.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Doe you know that name sir?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose:
Yes Lady so well, that I am sorry, that a gentlewoman
of your good seeming should haue to doe for so light a
peece of vanity. Leaue going o'the devills Errants: His
kingdomes large enough, and too much peopled already.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: Pray sir, are you in sober earnest?

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I good faith am I.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:
You are vnhappy then. For you shall loose, in this
disdaine of yours, more honour then your life time in repentance
can recover. So fare you well sir.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose:
Farewell old Whiskin. Slid Ile marry out o' the
way; tis time I thinke: I shall bee tane vp for whores meat
else. Constance! shee had a Bastard tother day too. What a
mischeiuous Maw has this shee Caniball that gapes for mee!
Slight a common Trader, with I know not how many! I
maruell shee was left out of Cupids Muster. Sure shee bribd
the Ballat-maker: One that I haue paid at all times too;
heres one, there's tother. And now shee heares I am towards
mariage pretends a claime to mee. And what a Minister
shee had procur'd! A Divell in a most gentlewomanlike
apparition. It had beene well to haue pumpd her. Is
shee gone?

speeches.speaker: Pate.
prose: Who sir, the Gentlewoman? I put her in her coach.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose:
Her Coache! Coaches must needs bee common,
when their cariages are so. By this light, Oliver, a Bawd; a
very Bawd. Where's my brother Widgine, and his Governour,
Anvile! They are wholsomer company o' the two,
yet.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose:
A Bawd I Blesse my Masters wits. But the best is, if
hee be mad, there's that at hand will tame him, or any man:
A fine Cooler, call'd Mariage, to take his batchelors button
a h^le lower! Can it bee possible? Shee might ha' beene
Mother o' the Maydes, as well, to my seeming; or a Matron,
to haue traind vp the best Lady Daughters in the Countrie.
Here comes her Man, againe.

speeches.speaker: Be.
prose: Is sir Phillip Lucklesse i' the house still sir?

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose:
Are you the Cock-bawd to the hen was here, ere
while sir.

speeches.speaker: Be.
prose: Are you mad, or are you drunke sir?

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose:
C^me you to bargaine for a Punke sir? Faith where's
the meeting? Wher's the Supper? at the Bridgefoot, or the
Cat? or where is it?

speeches.speaker: Be.
prose:
Nay then sir, though your Master be allowd to measure
his manners, by his pleasure, here, on his owne yard,
Ile bee bold to pull you out on't by the eares, and beat you
into better fashion.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose:
Hold, hold. Pray hold a little sir. I cry you mercy.
I might bee mistaken. I see thou art a good fellow. I haue
halfe a dozen for thee faith. S' foot what big words and terrible
action he has! Is this the Bawds language? Pray pardon
me sir: I haue beene overwatch'd of late, and knew neither
place, person, not what I said at the instant.

speeches.speaker: Be.
prose: Indeed?

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose:
I sir, tis an infirmity I am much troubled withall;
a kind of a—betweene steepe and waking—I know not what
to call it. I would giue tvventie nobles to bee cured on't.
I pray take it not ill sir; I vse any man so, when the fits on



mee, till they throughly wake mee.

speeches.speaker: Be.
prose:
What as I did now? by the eares? Are you come
to your selfe enough yet? or shall I helpe you further sir?

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose:
No, tis very well now I thanke you sir. Alas I put
my Master to the paines, twise or thrise a weeke, I assure you,
to my griefe.

speeches.speaker: Be.
prose: A very strange disease! How might you get it?

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose:
Faith I fell into 't first, with a conceit I tooke for
overbuying a bargaine of Drinke. Your businesse with my
Master sir? I pray.

speeches.speaker: Be.
prose:
Onely to speake with him from the Gentlewoman
was here eene now.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: I shall acquaint him with it.

speeches.speaker: Be.
prose: I shall be your seruant.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: I pray pardon my error.

speeches.speaker: Be.
prose: And you my boldnesse.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose:
O not so sir. Well master Pimp I haue a plot vpon
your imployment, as brauely as you carry it. I know he is
a Bawd by his out-facing. And I doe humble and disguise
my Manhood to worke on him by policy: And if I put not
a fine^ slurre vpon him for all his braue brauados, then Oliver
Pate has no braines; nor is there any difference betwixt a
Seruing-man and a Pandar.—

speeches.speaker: Be.
prose:
What a Trim-tram trick is this? the Master and the
Man both brain-cras'd; as the one vsed me, so did the other
my Mistris. But I haue brought this into a kind of civill
sense againe. Doe wee looke like Bawds? There is some
strange ground for this mistaking. I am sure shee has ever
beene reputed a vertuous Gentlewoman; and has now the
governement, and bringing vp of a Virgin, of a most hopefull
goodnesse. And I thinke, I know my selfe; and dare
beat any Man into a better construction of my quality.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose:
Now wit, and bee thy will! Sir, my Master desires
to bee excused: for he is with some friends, on priuate busines,
concerning his Mariage; which is to be to morrow.
But sayes, if it please you to meet him in the Euening, betweene
foure, and fiue, in the great Pallace; and condnuct



him to the Gentlewoman, hee will attend her with his best
seruice.

speeches.speaker: Be.
prose:
Betweene foure, and fiue in the Pallace: but how
shall I know him? I neuer saw him.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose:
As I wish'd: But you may easily. Hee is of a comely
stature; and will be in a red cloa^e and a white Feather,
Besides Ile waite on him.

speeches.speaker: Be.
prose: I thanke you sir.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose:
Fare you well sir. Good Foist, I shall make a
Whiskin of you now, and for nothing too. I haue beene a
little bold with my Masters name in this answere; the knowledge
of which he is vnguilty of. I saw how he shifted her
off: Therefore I will further bee bold both with his name
and person, which I will put vpon a friend in store. My speciall
friend, Captaine Anvile, a notable lecherous Tuppe:
He has beene at me for a bit out of my Masters flocke any
time these three weekes. Ile pleasure him with her for ready
money. I know tis some cast stuffe, that my Master has
done withall. And let him take what followes.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: Well sir. And what said Master Lucklesse?

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: Sir Phillip you meane forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
The very same sir. But I beginne to call him now,
as I must call him hereafter. Ladies doe not call their husbands,
as they are Knights: as sir Phillip, sir Timothy, or sir
Gregory. Did you ever heare my Lady Squelch call her husband
sir Paul? No. But master Squelch. Indeed all others
must sir them by their Christen names; because they are
Knights, and to bee knowne from other men: onely their
owne wiues must master them, by their Sirnames; because
they are Ladies, and will not know them from other men.
But to our busines. What said he to you?

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: His worship said forsooth—

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
Nay, What said you to him first? I loue to heare
things in order.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: I said that as you bad me forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
As I bad you, Clotpoll? what was that? Shall I
ever mould thee into a Gentleman Vsher thinkst thou, that
stand'st so? Come forwards sir, and repeat.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose:
My Mistris commends her best loue vnto your Worship;
and desires to know how your Worship came home
last night; and how your Worship haue rested; and how
your Worship dos this morning? Shee hopes the best of
your Worships health; and would be glad to see your Worship
at your Worships best leasure.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
This was very well: word for word as I instructed.
But did you worship him so much?

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose:
Yes truly, and hee commended mee for it; and said I
shew'd my breeding.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: Now sir. His answere? in his owne words.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose:
Quoth hee. I thanke thy Mistris, and I thanke thee.
Prithee commend my seruice to her, and tell her, my worship
came home vpon my worships Foot-cloath; my worship
tooke very good rest, in my worships bed: My worship
has very little to doe this Morning, and will see her at
my worships leasure.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: Did hee say so?

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose:
Twas either so, or so much I am sure. But he did not
make me repeat, as you did, till I had cond it by heart.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
Well Howdie get you downe. And ^oe you heare
Howdee? If sir Paul Squelch come, bring him vp.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: I will forsooth Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: I bad you learne to call me Madame.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: I shall forsooth Ma-dame.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
You shall forsooth Madame. Tis but a day to't; and
I hope one may be a Lady one day before her time.

speeches.speaker: How.
prose: A day too soone ^ doubt in this forward age.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
In the meane time, let me study my remembrances
for after mariage.

Imprimis, To haue the whole sway of the house; and all
domesticall affaires; as of accounts of houshold chardges,
placing and displacing of all seruant^ in generall; To haue
free liberty, to goe on all my visits; and though my knights
occasions bee never so vrgent, and mine of no moment, yet



to take from him the command of his Coach; To be in speciall
fee with his best trusted seruant; nor to let one liue
with him, that will not bewray all his counsells to mee. To
study and practise the Art of iealousie; To faine anger, melancholly,
or sickn^sse, to the life. These are Arts that women
must bee well practis'd in, ere they can attaine to wisedome,
and ought to be the onely study of a widow, from the
death of her first husband, to the second: From the second
to the third, matters of deeper moment; From the third to
the fourth deeper yet; And so proportionably to the seauenth,
if shee be so long blest with life: But of these I may
finde time hereafter to consider in order as they fall. Besides,
in all, to be singular in our will; to raigne, gouerne, ordaine
lawes and breake 'hem, make quarrells and maintaine 'him;
professe truthes, deuise falshoods; protest obedience, but
study nothing more then to make our husbands so; Controle,
controuert, contradict, and be contrary to all conformity:
To which end wee must be sure to be arm'd alwayes
with prick and praise of the deceased; and cary the Inuentory
of our goods, and the grosse summe of our Dowry perpetually
in our mouthes. Then dos a husband tickle the
spleene of a woman, when shee can anger him to please him;
chide him to kisse him; Mad him to humble him; make
him stiffe necked to supple him; and hard-hearted to breake
him; to s^t him vp, and take him downe, and vp againe, and
downe againe, when, and as often as we list.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: Madame.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: I marry, now thou say'st well.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: Andt please your Ladiship.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: Well said againe.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose:
One M. Tridewell,
^ Gentleman, desires to speak with
your Ladiship, from Sir Phillip.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
Tridewell! O it is Sir Phillips Kinsman. I haue heard
him speake much good of him; and entreated mee to giue
him good respect; which were enought to marre his entertainment,
had I not another purpose of mine owne, that may
proue as ill. Bring him vp Howdee.

speeches.speaker: Ho.
prose: I will Madame—

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
I that was very well. This Howde^
doe I meane
with a cast Gowne to put in apparell, and make my Gentleman
Vsher; Not onely for the aptnesse of his name, to goe
on my visits; but for his proportionable talent of wit and
manners.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
If I can yet redeeme him, he is happy. By your leaue
Lady: May my boldnesse proue pardonable?

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
Sir the name of him, you come from, is warrant sufficient
to make your welcome here: All that is here being
his.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: Is this shee trow!

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: I vnderstand you come from Sir Phillip Luckles.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
'Tis true, I brought his name thus farre to enter mee
to your presence. But here I shake it off, as I would doe his
remembrance: but that I know him too well.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: Too well Sir? How meane you?

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
Too well indeede Lady; but in the ill part. I know
him to be no equall Match for you. Yet I heare you receiue
him as a Suter.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: Right Sir. and him onely.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: It is not gone so farre I hope.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
Beshrew mee but it is; and farther too Sir. Hee has
all wooed and wonne me.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
verse: Beshrew your fortune then. And if my coun^ell;
The friendliest counsell e're you hearkned to,
Stop not your ventrous foote from one step further,
(For now you are vpon the brinke of danger)
You fall into a Sea of endlesse sorrowes.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
verse: This is pretty!

speeches.speaker: Tri.
verse: Looke back into your selfe; read o're your Story,
Finde the content the quiet minde you liu'd in,
The wealth, the peace, the pleasure you enioy'd;
The free command of all you had beneath you,
And no^e to be commanded by aboue you.
Now glaunce your eye on this side, on the yoake,
You bring your neck to, l^den downe with cares,
Where you shall faintly draw a tedious life,
And euery step incounter with new strife.
Then, when you groane beneath your burdenous charge,
And wearily chance to reuert a looke
Vpon the price you gaue for this sad thraldome,
You'll feele your heart stabd through with many a woe,
Of which one dyes not while a thousand grow.
All will be then too late: Now is the time,
Now rings the warning bell vnto your breast:
Where if you can but entertaine a thought,
That tells you how you are beset with danger,
You are secu^e; Exclude it, you are lost
To endlesse so^rowes, bought with dearest cost.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
verse: Pray Sir deale freely with me. What respect
Moues you to make this strong disswasion?
Is it your care of me? or loue of him?

speeches.speaker: Tri.
verse: A subtill question! This woman is not brainelesse.
Loue of him Lady? If this can be loue,
To seeke to crosse him, in so great a hope,
As your inioying; being all the meanes,
Or possibility he has to liue on;
If it be loue to him, to let you know
How lewd and dissolute of life he is,
By which his fortunes being sunke, he is growne
The scorne of his acquaintance, his friends trouble,
B^ing the common borrower of the Towne.
A Gallant lights not a Iobacco Pipe,
But with his bor^owing letters (shee's not mou'd)
And if you put him off a fortnight longer,
Hee^l be layd vp for moneys he tooke vp
To buy his Knighthood; besides his deepe ingagements
To Goldsmith, Silkman, Taylor, Millener,
Sempster, Shoomaker, Spurrier, Vintner, Tapster,
(All stirres her not, shee stands as if prepar'd
To heare as much of truth and beare with it.)
Men of all Trades, and Occupations,
From his Mercer downward to his Waterman,
Haue venter'd the last sixpence on his Credit;
And all but wayt to pay themselues from you.
And I may well imagine how't would grieue
A woman of your wealth, to disburse all,
To saue a Knight out of his Ward i'th' Counter;
And lack with all his company at home;
While he frequents youthfull society
To make more charge for Nurseries abroad:
For I haue heard him say you are old; and that
It is your wealth he marries, ^d not you.
If this be loue to him, that I discouer
(The meanes to saue you to be his vndoing,)
Let no man take a friends help in hi^ wooing.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
verse: And how this should proceed from care of me
Falls not into my vnderstanding Sir.

speeches.speaker: Tri
verse: Consid^r Lady—

speeches.speaker: Fit.
verse: Sir I haue consider'd
Before, and in your speech, and since; and cannot
By all that can be said remoue a thought.
I lou'd him not for words: Nor will I vse
Words against yours: 'twere poore expression
Of loue to boast it. Tis enough I know it.
Boasters of loue, how can we Louers call,
When most of such loue one no more then all.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: Sure, I was much mistaken in this woman.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
verse: Nor would I haue you to expect a rayling,
To say you basely wrong the Gentleman:
A way so common, common women vse it.
But this Sir I will say, I were too blame
If I should thinke your loue to him were lesse
Then the great care of me, you seeme to vrge,
As you pretend it is.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
verse: Shee will discouer me.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
verse: You are his Kinseman nearly; and reputed,
By his owne mouth, his best of chosen friends;
My selse an vtter stranger, one from whom
You neuer had, or can expect least good.
And why you should, for a respect so contrary,
Call my poore wit in question to beleeue you,
Is most vnconscionable.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
verse: Me thinke I stand
Like a false witnes 'gainst anothers life,
Ready to take his punishment.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
verse: Nor will I foudly thinke you meant to seeke,
Crossing his Match, to make it for your selfe:
Both for my knowen unworthinesse; and your
Deprauing him being no possible way
To make me thinke the better of your worth.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
verse: Can this be shee? how strangely am I taken!

speeches.speaker: Fit.
verse: But I forgiue, and charitably thinke
All this brought no ill purpose; pretty Pageantry
Which may hereafter, 'mong our mariage mirth,
Fill vp a Scene: for now Ile take no notice.
Indeed I will not: you may, if you please,
And tell your Cuz how haynously I take it.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
verse: If thou hast mercy, Loue, keep't from my heart.
Wil't please you heare me?

speeches.speaker: Fit.
verse: Sir I haue, enough.
And craue but leaue to speake this little to you,
Which shall by heauen be vncontrol'd as Fate.
If I shall find him bad, I'le blame my fortune:
Neuer repent or thanke you for your counsell.
If I shall finde him good; and all this false,
VVhich you so violently haue vrg'd against him;
Ile loue him nere the more, nor you the worse:
For I am not so poore, nor weakly spiritted,
That should all friends to whom my faith is bound,
Say on their knowledge, that all this were true,
And that one houres protraction of our Mariage
Should mak't appeare, that I would giue allowance
To all their bugbeare reasons, to deferre
That houre the vniting of our hands: because
Our hearts are link'd by the Diuinest lawes.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
verse: What haue I done? The curse of ouer-weening brains,
Shame, and disgrace are guerdon of my paines.
O, I shall fall beneath the scorne of fooles:
A punishment as iust, as great for such,
That doe in things, concerne them not, too much.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
verse: What ayles the Gent?

speeches.speaker: Tri.
verse: O^ what a setled rock of Constancie
She planteth her affection? not to moue,
Though all the breath of sl^nderous reproach,
Driuing tempestuous clowds and stormes of horror,
Should beat, at once, against it.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
verse: Sir How dee?

speeches.speaker: Ho.
verse: Ma-dame.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
verse: Not you Sir.

speeches.speaker: Tri
verse: I would I had not seene, at least not heard her
In all so contrary to all opinion.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
verse: You are not well Sir.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
verse: They said she was old, vnhandsome, and vnc^uill,
Forward, and full of womanish distemper.
Shee's none of these: but opposite in all.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
verse: Sir.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
verse: My witty purpose was to saue my friend
From such a hazard; and to loath her so,
That I might make her loathsome to his fansie:
But I my selfe am falne into that hazard;
To wrong my friend; to burne in lawlesse lo^e;
Which oh that prayers or penance may remoue.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
verse: You are not going Sir?

speeches.speaker: Tri.
verse: I beg your pardon; dare not look vpon you.—

speeches.speaker: Fit.
verse: Gone in a dreame. Well, I perceiue this iugling.
This straine was onely to explore the strength
Of my affection to my lucklesse Knight.
For which, if both their Cunnings I not fit,
Let me be call'd the barren wife of wit.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
The strangenes of this Gentlemans action will not out
of my mind yet. Sir Phillip could not but haue a hand in it.
Do's he repent his bargaine already; and desire to bee quit
with losse of his earnest? Tis but his faith and troth.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
Sister, where are you? My Governour and I are
come to waite vpon you in sir Phillip Lucklesse coach. It
waits at doore for you; and what to doe thinke you?

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
I can not tell. Perhaps to inuite me forth into the
ayre of
^ideparke or Maribone; or else—

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
Or else me no or elses, sister, you cannot guesse it.
And I was a foole to aske you the question, now I think on't.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: That was well remembred brother.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
Sister, you are to be a Lady, within this halfe houre.
Your knight is ready, so is the Parson too. My Gouernour
here knowes.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose:
Yes Lady; and that hee intreats you, to beare with
the sodain^sse of the occasion, which hee protests, deepely
vrges him to be married presently; desiring you not to trouble
your selfe in examination of his reasons: for vpon his
honesty and honour, the end of it is for good to you both.
Come sweet Madame (now I am bold to giue you your dew
title) your knight is ready prest on his aduontures (dee heare)
and tis onely you, that hee seekes to incounter.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
There's a iest now: but shee vnderstands it not.
He makes her an Infidell, a wild beast or a Monster, by that
word Incounter; what doe Knights adventurers incounter
else? looke all the Mirror over. Hee'll incounter her. O the
wit of a Gouernour!

speeches.speaker: An.
prose:
Tis as I say Madame, (dee heare) the good fit's come
on him.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
Ever at the tayle of his dee heare, I am sure to
smell a iest: the fits come on him:

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
This sodaine importunity confirmes my former
doubt: He thinkes his Scare-crow will make me keepe off



now; but hee is cossend. Well sir. He shall find me obedient
to his hand. I am in all prepar'd to meet his purposes;
Though, Brother I had thought to had conference this Morning
with sir Paul Squelch touching a match for you.

speeches.speaker: VVid.
prose:
For me sister: ha' you found out a wi^e for me?
ha' you? pray speake, ha' you?

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
And a good match too brother; Sir Pauls Neece:
on whom, hee, being childles, meanes to bestow a large
Dowry.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
Fit.
prose:
Hee is a right good man. Within there.

Bid Flaps your fellow bring my Fan and Masque.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose:
Is hee bounteous and liberall ha? Do's he make large
Suppers and lend money. Dee heare? Is he good at that?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
Nay, there you mistake Gouernour. A good man
i'th Citty is not call'd af^er his good deeds, but the knowne
weight of his purse. One, whose name any Vsurer can
read without spectacles; One that can take vp more with
two fingers and a thombe vpon the Exchange, then the
great man at Court, can lift with both his hands; One that
is good onely in riches, and weares nothing rich about him
but the Gout, or a thombe Ring with his Grandsites sheepmarke,
or Grannams butter-print on't, to seale bags, acquittanc^s
and Counternanes.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: A Butter-print?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
I twere a cunning Herald could find better Armes
for some of 'hem: though I haue heard ^r Paul Squelch
protest he was a gentleman, and might quarter a coat by his
Wiues side. Yet I know hee was but a Grasier when he left
the Countrey; And my Lord his father whistled to a teame
of horses (they were his owne indeed.) But now hee is
right worshipfull, and I would I had his Neece vnsight and
vnseene I faith for her monies sake. You neuer heard mee
aske if shee were faire or hansome, dee marke that sister?
My fathers rule right. And if I be not a true Widgine. (God
forgi' me) I thinke he was none.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
But shee is very faire brother, and very hansom^
and the prettiest innocent countrey thing withall. Doe I
want nothing here?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: I now you bring me to bed sister.

speeches.speaker: May.
prose: Your Masque sits well forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: But where's my Wimple forsooth?

speeches.speaker: May.
prose: Vpon the Cupboards head, pray Humfrey fetch it.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
Hee liues not that loues a Countrey thing like me.
Alas none loues a Countrey thing l^ke mee. And though I
am a Cockney, and was neuer further then Hammersmith;
I haue read the Countrey mans common wealth; and can discourse
of Soccage and Tenure, Free-hold, Copy-hold; Lease,
Demeanes, Fee-simple and Fee-taile, Plowing, Hedging,
Diking, Grubbing, occupying any Countrey thing whatsoeuer;
and take as much pleasure in't, as the best Clowne
borne of 'h^m all.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
verse: And shee is very young, ^ aboue fifteene, brother.
How this fellow stayes! Goe you.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose:
And that's a safe age for a Maid in the countrey: dee
heare?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
Pardon me Gouernour. I doe heare and not heare
thee at this time.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: And sings, and speakes so pretty northenly they say.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose:
Is shee Northern (dee heare) will shee not shrinke
i' the wetting?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
Gouernour, I know thou spokst a iest now, by thy
dee heare: but prithee forgiue me; I cannot applaud nor
marke thee at this time.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
What mak^s you stay so? I feare you haue beene
among my sweet meats.

speeches.speaker: How.
prose:
Shee said it was vpon the Cupboard; and it was
vnder the Cupboard.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
Is this my Wimple? Doe you bring Carpenters
tooles to dr^sse me withall.

speeches.speaker: Ma.
prose: Here is your Wimple forsooth.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
I sh^ll teach you to know a difference betweene



gentlewomens geere and Carpenters tooles. I shall

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
Nay, shee is so vext now I Deare sister to the Countrey
Lasse againe. You said, she spoke and sung Northernly.
I haue a great many Southerne songs already. But Northern
ayres nips it dead. Yorke Yorke for my money.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
Yes brother shee is Northern, and speakes so: for
shee has euer liu'd in the Countrey, till this last weeke, her
Vncle sent for ^er vp to make her his child, cut of the Bishoprick
of Durham.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Bishop, nor Bishoprick shall hold her from mee.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: And brother—

speeches.speaker: Wid.
verse: And so in height of complement grow compleat
More goes to making of a Man, the^ meat.
prose:
S^ster no mo^e, though I haue never seene her.
No Bishoprick i'th' land from me shall winne her. If you
will goe, and clap hands with your knight, come; I would
see you matchd first: because that will add some honour
to the Widgine^, when my selfe shall bee brother to a Lady.
I shall write first of that name. And then am I no sooner
married, Gouernour, but wee will set our trauels a foot: to
know Countries, and Nations, Sects and Factions, Men and
Manners; Language and Behauiour.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:
Pray tell me; and tell me truely. What is the most
has past betweene you? I^ it bee the maine losse of your
Mayden-head, it shall neare go further: the^efore let mee
know it.

speeches.speaker: Con
prose:
As I liue Mistris Trainewell, all that ere he had o'me
was but a kisse. But I mun tell yee, I wish'd it a thoosnnd,
thoosand till him.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: How often haue you seene him?

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose:
Feath but that bare eance nother, and your seln
were by too. Trow yee that Ide not tell yee and twere maer.
By my conscience Mrs. Trainewell I lee not.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:
That once that I saw him with you, your V^cle



was there, too, in the Orchard, but last weeke.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose:
Vary true, Mine Vncle was than by too. And hee
brought sir Phillip to see his Orchard. And what did hee
than doe, trow you, but tuke me thus by th' haund, and thus
hee kust mee; hee sed I were a deaft Lasse: but ther he feind.
But for my life I could not but thinke, he war the likest man
that I had seene with mine eyne; and could not devaise the
thing I had, might be vnbeggen by him. Then by and by as
we walkd, he askd mine Vncle, gin hee would giue him me
to make a Lady till him. And by my trouth Mistris Trainwell,
I lee not, I blush'd and luk'd vpon him as I would feine a hed
it so: Mine Vncle said yes, and sir Phillip shuke my haund,
and gude feath my heart ioyd at it. God gin the Priest had
beene by. But I thought all sure enough; and would not ha'
sold my part for the Spanish Ladies Ioincture. But streight
anon mine Vncle and he fell on other talke, of Lords and Ladies,
and many foud like things, I minded not: For I is weell
sure, this keept me waking ere sine. And God pardon mee
what I misthought euery houre i'th' night.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:
How haue you made me wrong this Gentleman, to
challenge him as if hee had beene your due vpon this idle
complement? when I vndertooke the Message, I presum'd
(for so your words did intima^e to me) you had beene sure,
as fast as faith could bind you, man and wife. Where was
my discretion? Now I perceiue this was but common
Courtship; and no assurance of a Mariage promise.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose:
I wot not what he meant. But I is weell sure, Ile nere
bee sure to ony Man but hee. And if hee loue mee not as
weell, God pardon him. For I meant him none ill.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:
I know not how to counsell or comfort you, vntill I
heare him speake. My man tells me, hee appointed him to
meet, and bring him to you about this houre. Poore heart I
pitty thee. Before thou come to halfe my yeares thou wilt
forget to loue halfe so truely.

speeches.speaker: Bea.
prose: Mistris.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: O, are you come? where's the Knight?

speeches.speaker: Bea.
prose:
He stayes below, and wild me to come vp first, to
to make his passage cleare and secure.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: That was discretion.

speeches.speaker: Bea.
prose:
Rather feare I thinke: for he ask'd me if the house
were not much haunted with Roarers or Swaggerers, poniards
and pistols: whether there were not an Assurer for it as
vpon the Exchange, as i^ his life were vpon hazard? whether
a Man might come on without losse of credit, and off
without need of a Surgeon? Much odd talke hee deliuers;
that in my conceit bewrayes, at once, both a ^asciuious and
cowardly disposition; and vpon my vnderstanding, ca^not
bee so generous, or nobly spirited, as hee is receiued. Doe
what you will.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: I suspect something.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: Will hee not come Mrs. Trainewell?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:
Yes sweetheart. But goe you to your Chamber
and let me haue a word before you see him. Goe call him in.
Doe so swetheart. Ile not be long.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose:
Ile doe ought you bid me God gin I saw him
eance.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose:
A place of faire promising! How haue I liu'd that
never discouer'd this place before? This place royall! But
sought my recreation, in by-lanes, and sluttish corners, vnsauory
Allies and Ditch sides? when here the whole house is
perfum'd: An Earle might thinke it his owne lodging;
Ladies might come to see the pictures, and not blush, to goe
in or out vnmask'd.

speeches.speaker: Bea.
prose:
Sir, will you speake to my Mistris? The man is
transported sure!

speeches.speaker: An.
prose:
I vnderstand thy office, leads thee no further; thy
paines are abroad and below stayres. Here honest Fetch.
Looke thee, heres the poore price of a new paire of shooes;
take it. Descend, and execute thy duty.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Blesse me! this is another man. More abuse yet?

speeches.speaker: An.
prose:
Now gentlevvoman to you. What fees belong to
your Key? Come, vvher's the bed? vvhere's the party?



Here's the man: her^'s the money. Chunke chunke you old
Gamster, dost heare? Here's halfe a peece to buy t^ee complection,
sack or Aqua-vitae. What thou lik'st.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: What are you sir I pray?

speeches.speaker: An.
prose:
Faith one thats a little ill giuen at this time. Where's
the ^ece? here are the peeces ^ tell thee.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:
What peece sir? If you can imagine what you are,
where you are, what you would haue, or where you would
be, I pray tell mee sir. ^le doe the best I can to satisfie you.
O' my discretion will I sir.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose:
Giue me but a little space to wonder at thy strange
demands and I wil tell thee, good discretion. If I should purchase
a broken Cock^combe, or bruz'd ribs now, for mistaking
another mans habit, the smart were onely mine. The
villaine swore to me, his Master was sent for; and that his
Master swore this w^s a Bawd to his choyce Whore, newly
intertayn'd; and that shee knew not him, and might well
mistake me for him. On which presumption I ha^e waded
thus farre: and if I sticke in the Mud, or be driuen backe by
a tempest, I am armd. Tis not the first time I haue beene
Wether-beaten, or Dry-beaten, dee heare?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Sir.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose:
You doe not know me? or, at least, not remember
mee?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:
If I erte therein sir, I hope your pardon. For as
you shall reueale your selfe, I shall either repent me of my
obliuion, or accuse you of vnaduisednesse.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose:
Shee speakes like the wife of an Orator, that could
dictate her husbands speeches! Were not you this Morning
at sir Phillip Lucklesse lodging? spoke not you with
him? sent you not for him afterwards to repaire hither to
the party? And know you not the man?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:
O infinite abuse! Sir I cry you mercy. I hope you
will pardon my weake sightednes. The worlds ^ad and we

prose:

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:

—

prose:

speeches.speaker: Fitc.

speeches.speaker: Tri.

prose:

prose:

prose:

speeches.speaker: Bul.
prose:

prose: As how sir?

prose:

prose:

speeches.speaker: An.
prose:

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:

^ee the second time? It lookes as it had beene once his

speeches.speaker: Pate.
prose:
Out of her wits say they? I feare shee is ^ then

speeches.speaker: Tray.
prose: They are falne out I thinke.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose:
O Mrs. Traynwell, for deare Charities ^ake ha' me soone^



^ this Man: for I'le nere take ony thing at him. Hee talkes

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose:
By my faith you wrong me: Nor of any poysoning purpo^e.
I was but putting a case of—

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose:
Pray put vp your Pipes sir. I like not your Musicke:

yee sir.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: Is that the Gent?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Yes sir. Pray obserue. But how fell you out sir?

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose:
I must first ^alute him by your favo^r. Sir, all the accumul^tions
of honour showre downe vpon you.

speeches.speaker: Luc
prose:
S^r. May you r^pe the vvhole harvest of your fruitfull
wishes.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: Deare sir, keep^ further fro' him.

speeches.speaker: Pate.
prose:
But one vvord sweet Lady; and you shall haue the
vvhole benefit of h^s presence to your s^lfe.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: ^e not afraid sweet-heart, he dares not hurt sir Phillip.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: In ^roth he breathes to neare him.

speeches.speaker: Tra
prose:
^ wa^rant y^u. What has hee done to m^ue her thus?
I know not what thi^
^ Doctor is. But M. Tridewell put

speeches.speaker: Pate.
prose: Your C^ach is ready at dore you say.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Ye^ my most d^licate Doctor.

speeches.speaker: Pate.
prose:
As you finde her then after a few vvords away vvith

speeches.speaker: Con
prose: But one word call yee this?

speeches.speaker: Pate.
prose:
I ha' done sweet soule. Lady I haue instructed the gent.
shall we l^au^ th^m?

speeches.speaker: Tr^.
prose:
One vvord, by your leaue first M. Doctor, and I'le attend

Kin^mans word, my Complotter in this busines. Therefore

hath appointed, till the Eueni^g; and let me

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: My life and honour be her Guard, and your security.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:
No more sir. Ile lay no coniurations vpon so noble a
spirit. Come Master Doctor—

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: But doe you loue me Constance?

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: O right weell sir.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: And will you be my Woman?

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: I is sure, ile nener be mine owne els^.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose:
But you will not goe away with m^c now, if I request
you?

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose: Any whither but to bed before wee be married.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose:
What from your Gouernesse, your Vncle, and all the
World?

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose:
And thanke you too sir. And ta' mee but fro' this ill
looking Doctor; for I shall be weell with you sir.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose:
Come, since you trust me so well, wee two will not
part till wee are lawfully made one.

speeches.speaker: Con.
prose:
Heauen blisse the houre you speake in, and all Saints
be with^sses.

speeches.speaker: Squ
prose: Where's this Doctor? where's this melancholly Gentlewoman?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: O me is hee come?

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: Is this her Vncle?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: E^en he sir. Where's my charge; Mistris Constance?

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: S^ue yee sir Ile goe find her—

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:
Where's my charge? Ile goe find her! What's the
meaning?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:
Shee was here but now sir, while the Musick plaid.
And wee withdrew our sclues, thinking she might sleepe sir.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose: There went a Coach away as I came in. Whole was it?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: A C^ach sir? Alas I am affraid; my flesh trembles.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:
At what in your great Master the Diuels name?
Where's my Ncece?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:
Sir here came in one Master Widgine, the Lady Luckt^s
brother—

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose: Well.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: As acquainted with the Doctor sir—

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose: VVell, well.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:
And he saw her sir. But seem'd to depart, when wee
withdrew our selues to talke about the cure.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:
Very very well. While you were wisely talking about
the cure, a Widgine flies away with the Patient. Where's
this Doctor? Doctor I say. Doctor! Hee's run away too, my
life on't. A meere plot, a Conspiracie; tis so directly, below
there. I can not see how it can bee otherwise.
Saw you the Doctor? Yes sir, hee went now forth at the water-Gate,
and tooke boat in hast.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:
Exceeding well. How came your Discretion acquainted
with this Doctor?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:
Sir he was reported to me by very good Iudgements,
to be a rare Practitioner.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:
A most rare fellow, and do's admirable tricks, by slight
of heeles. But I may perhaps out-run 'hem—

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:
My purge workes as I wisht. I am amus'd though at
the flight of the Doctor. But I haue too many businesses to intertaine
new thoughts.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
May I belceue it, Good sir? may I be so happy, that my
brother has her?

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
As I haue truth in me, I am most credibly told so. Mary
the worst is, her Vncle is so mad at their escape, th^t hee will
neuer giue consent to the match, whereby her portion will bee
lesse.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
Hang him Clod. My will shall be a portion su^ficient
to my brother, I care not, though hee giue her not a penny, so
VVat has the Wench.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
Make you noe more doubt of that, then I doe Madame,
who haue vpon the report of it already, prepard the
Learned of the Ciuill Law, those that you nominated of your
good acquaintance, and are forward to doe you the best office,



who haue appointed to meet before the Iu^ge of the Archdeaacous
Court p^esent^y, whither I haue promised to bring, and
will attend you.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: But the other side must be summond by processe.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
Sir Phill^p hath wa^ning already M^dame; and without

co^ming. So that my selfe and his serua^t, who haue neuer

i^ Law. So that all will be euded in three whispers. Ods
pitty, looke who here is.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose: O are you here my Lady Lu kiesse?

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
Twas time you found me sir; you might ha'mistaken
my name else. F^r withi^ this heure, ^ m^ght haue retu^'d
the ancient title of your friend, and Awdery F^tchow.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose: Slow wov, where is my N^?

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
Where are your wits si^? you come vpon me inde^d ^
What Neece? What's the matter?

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:
My Neece Censtance, that your brother Widgi^e stole
from the Doctor, and is stowne away witha^. But hee must not

D^coy, before they be coupled, as sure as your Ladiship or

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: Sure the old Gentleman is fallen mad. What hath happend?

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:
The plot smels of your Ladiships policy; you^ Ladiships
Lilly white fist is t^ule in t^e busines. But I will haue a

and alliance in the Whatshical. Court No^b^

^
^our^
^ there must not cary it, my great Lady. Directly it

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
Your ^re an vnciuill greasie Co^panion, to vpbraid and

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
O good Madarne, hurt not your selfe with anger

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
Hee makes me forget my selfe by his example. Sir you

You spend too much breath in these lowd noates, very hurtfull

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
Will you beleeue mee sir? you may: For tis Truth, as I

^evvoman:

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:

prose:

prose:

prose: O^t you Curry-combe.

prose: I will be so reueng'd—

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: How pray?

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:

^ld deuise to punish, then if I take him to suffer vnder my

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: Ha, ha, ha.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: What thinke you of your Brothers successe, now Madame?

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: Looke you now Madame. See who here come^.

prose:

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: Shee is a Holdup her selfe, if I mistake not her name.

prose:

speeches.speaker: Hold.
prose:

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:

speeches.speaker: Hold.
prose: I would be glad and twere so.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:

speeches.speaker: How.
prose: I hope I perform'd my duty.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Which wee must not see vnrewarded sister.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:

speeches.speaker: How.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: I thanke you sir.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:

tooke her into an inner too me, to make all sure, as well within
as without; and I so phillipt her—

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: Enough brother, no more. I vnderstand you.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:

It passeth your vnderstanding and mine too, the delight of it.

Oh what a delight shee gaue me. And how light I am after
^
Heigh. My pretty sweet Rascall.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: Enough I say.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:

gone sor a Licence.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: So, ha you done now?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Ile vndertake—

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: Yet againe.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:

pleasant, I doubt not.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Oh I could liue and dye in this discourse sir.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: Lady doe you thinke of the time?

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
I will instantly along vvith you. Hewdee come you
vvith me. Brother, the search hath past this house already.
You any goe in vvith your Svveet-heart, and stay here safely.
Goe in, and keepe close, till I send to meet me at Supper.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: In and in sister, and be close enough, seare not—

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: Now sir when you please.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: I am your seruent Lady—

speeches.speaker: Vex.
prose:

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:

speeches.speaker: Vex.
prose:

speeches.speaker: Nons.

speeches.speaker: Bea.
prose:

speeches.speaker: Non.
prose: H^ you any Whitpots?

prose:

This great Supper or ^ast (as I may properly call it) was

speeches.speaker: Non.
prose: To try is he would forget it or no?

speeches.speaker: B^a.
prose:

speeches.speaker: Non.
prose: But what must I say to 'hem?

speeches.speaker: Bea.
prose:

speeches.speaker: Bul.
prose: Your Master abroad and not within say you?

speeches.speaker: Clea.
prose:
Yes. But good sir stay his comming, I pray you, for
his good.

speeches.speaker: Bul.
prose:
I partly apprehend you at full. Mistris Traynwell appointed

speeches.speaker: Non.
prose:
Onely salute 'hem, bid' hem welcome. Tell'hem Sir

prose: Loue has made you a Courtier. M Nonsense

speeches.speaker: Non.
prose: No I protest and vow. I doe but speake as they say.—

speeches.speaker: Bea.
prose: What haue you said Sir?

speeches.speaker: Non.
prose: What you said I haue an ill verbatim else.

speeches.speaker: Bea.
prose:
I said but the meaning of what you should say, and put

speeches.speaker: Non.
prose: No sir. I will take your owne vvords for this matter.

speeches.speaker: Bea.
prose: I am beholden to you.

speeches.speaker: Clea.
prose:
I am glad Fortune has sent one man of Civill government

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Saue you sir. Are you the Worshipfull of the house?

speeches.speaker: Bul.
prose: I apprehend you sir.—

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: How sir?—

speeches.speaker: Bul.
prose:
Mistake me not I beseech you, I apprehend you to be

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: You doe not mock me sir?

speeches.speaker: Bea.
prose: Sir, This is one of the Guests?

speeches.speaker: Non.
prose: Onely salute 'hem. Bid 'hem vvelcome—

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: What's this?

speeches.speaker: Non.
prose:
Tell 'hem Sir Paule vvas hastily call'd forth on his Maiesties

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Is this a Parrat or a Popingay?

speeches.speaker: Non.
prose: Entreat their patience till his return, which you know.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Doe you know vvhat you say sir?

speeches.speaker: Non.
prose:
Will be very sodaine, although you know not where
hee is—

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: If I did I vvould not seeke him here sir.

speeches.speaker: Non.
prose: And so forth as occasion serues.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose:
This is some inchaun^ed P^ace, and the people are
charm'd. I haue mistaken the house sure.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
Where's this hospitable Knight that invites Strangers. I
meane meere Strangers, that hee knowes not. Shew me the Lad
of bounty. I hunger not for his Sapper as I doe to salute him.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose:
Hee vvill proue the greatest stranger here himselfe I
thinke, for he is not at home sir. I am a Guest as you are, and
vvould be as glad to see him.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: He dos not meane to ieare vs dos he?

speeches.speaker: Bea.
prose:
I bese^ch you mistake not so his purpose sir: which is
faire vvelcome, and good cheare to you all. Therefore Gentlemen
and ladies, vvill it please you to entertaine one another
a while. Look yee.
Here's good Sack, and good I'obacco. And before the rest of
the Guests b^co^e, Sir Paule vvill be here himselfe.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: This fellow speakes.

speeches.speaker: Bul.
prose:
As I am a Iustice of Peace I cannot apprekend, and yet
me thinks I doe. What sort of people these Gentlemen may
be. See: more I Is sir Paule turn'd swaggerer? Or is his house
abus'd by servants? I vvill not leaue it, vntill they goe out before
mee like a layle deliuery. They lo^ke like men betwixt a
Repriue and Pardon. Friend: Are these sir Paules elected
friends?

speeches.speaker: Bea.
prose: His protected friends sir.

speeches.speaker: Bul.
prose: Protected?

speeches.speaker: Bea.
prose:
I sir. There is a fraternity of them. The brothers of



the Protect. There's not a man of 'hem, but has all Mayors,
Sheriffes, Bayliffes, Sergeants at Mace, Marshalls men, Constables,
and other his Maiesties Officers, in a Combcase in his pocket.
They are a Generation that never eate but in Parliament
time, and now every table is full of them.

speeches.speaker: Bul.
prose:
I should wonder what they did here else. See. A roaring
Doctor too, broke out o' the Kings Bench.

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose:
By your leaue Gallants. I perceiue your Company is
not yet full.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: Are you of the invited sir?

speeches.speaker: Pat.
prose:
It is not to be doubted sir. Yet a Voluntary. But there
are some without that are more then invited, yet come against
their wills.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: How meane you M. Doctor?

speeches.speaker: Pa
prose:
Brought sir by a Constable and Officers, to be examin'd.
Where's the iolly Iustice?

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: What are they can yee tell sir?

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: A Gentlewoman, and a Spaniard.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose: A Spaniard, Ha!

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: I, a Spaniard, Ha: if you will haue it so:

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose:
If we had but a Iustice among vs to Examine 'hem, it
might passe the time well till sir Paule came.

speeches.speaker: Bea.
prose:
Sir, here is a Iustice, and for the same purpose too for
ought we know, that shall not resuse to doe it, and in sir Paules
Gowne and Cap too.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: This is a witty fellow.

speeches.speaker: Bea.
prose:
Sir, you cannot doe a more acceptable office for your
friend, then to execute his place in his absence. Your anthority
makes you capable of it; and I doe the rather perswade it, because
the Gentlemen whom you wisely suspect for loose person^,
may see some example of Iustice; which may preuent
some present euill in their stay here.

speeches.speaker: Bul.
prose:
I apprehend you friend. Giue mee the Gowne and
Chayre, and let the Delinquents approach. Vmh, vmh.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Tis a Spaniard indeede.

speeches.speaker: Vex.
prose:
An English Spaniard sir, And therefore the verier



knaue: as will bee prou'd I doubt not, to his shame, and my renowne
in the Common ^. By your Worships leaue.

speeches.speaker: Bul.
prose: What newes b^ing ^ou M. Constable?

speeches.speaker: Vex.
prose:
Spanish newes sir. Wi^t please your Worship to examine
the vertue of my Warrant, and then these Persons aecordingly?

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:
Very good! I am brought before my selfe to bee examin'd,
and before a fine rable too! how the deuill brok this vnknowne
N^tion into my house, or doe not I mistake it? My
foolery has led me into a fine predicament. I will not yet disclose
my selfe: but looke a little surther towards the event.

speeches.speaker: Bul.
prose: Are you a Spa^iard sir?

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose: Such a one as you see Signior.

speeches.speaker: Bul.
prose:
See Signior. Hee speakes nothing but Spanish. The
question will be how we shall vnderstand this Examinant.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose: Hey day!

speeches.speaker: Bul.
prose:
I do see Signior I thanke the light, that you are a goodly
man of outward parts, and ezcept it were the black Knight
himselfe, or him with the Fistula, the proprest man I haue seene
of your Nation. They are a People of very spare dyet, I haue
^eard, and therefore seldome fat. Su^e you you haue had most
of your br^eding in this C^untrey, the dyet whereof you like
better then your own, which makes you linger here, after all
you Country men, vpon ^ome vn^ouch plot. And I shall wonder
therefore how you can speake no English. Can you speake
no English at all sir? Answere me I pray.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:
Not an English word not I s^. Alasse I haue not been
siue ^ayes in the K^ngio^e.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: This is exc^llent!

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: I, peace Y u'll marre all if you laugh.

speeches.speaker: Bul.
prose:
^, what shall wee doe then? Gentlemen, haue any
of you any Spanish, to helpe mee to vnderstand this strange
S^a^get?

speeches.speaker: T^i.
prose: Not a Riall sir not I.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose:
Nor a Rialls worth amongst vs of any language but
sh^er^ English.

speeches.speaker: Bul.
prose:
What S^iere of our Nation is next to Spaine? Perhaps
he may vnd^rst^nd that Shi^r, English.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: Deuonshire or Corn^all sir.

speeches.speaker: N^n.
prose:
Neuer credit me, but I will spowt some Cornish at him.
Peden bras vidne whee his cregas.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:
Am I transform' ^ vtterly? Is my Language alter'd with
my apparell, or are you all mad? what vnspeakeable misery is this.

speeches.speaker: Bull.
prose:
I see we shall neuer vnderstand, nor doe good on him, till
hee be instructed in the English tongue.

speeches.speaker: Vex.
prose:
And please your worship, the best Vniuersity for this purpose
will be Bridewell. I am acquainted with the best Tutors there,
Master Cleanewhip, Master Dri^lash, and diuers others.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose: You o^licious Rascall, are you mad?

speeches.speaker: Vex.
prose:
No such matter sir. But in my right mind, and Midlesex
feare it not.

speeches.speaker: Bull.
prose:
It must be so. His instruction will cost litle there, if hee
be not too old to learne. Therefore set him by, and let mee fall vpon
the Gentlewoman.

speeches.speaker: Vex.
prose: Oh, hee's rarely vext.

speeches.speaker: Bull.
prose: Now Gentlewoman, will it please you to be vnmasqu'd.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Yes sir looke you, I dare shew my face.

speeches.speaker: Bull.
prose: Mistris Trainowell, as I apprehend.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
prose: Mistris Trainewell.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose: Trainewell!

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:
Euen shee Gentlemen, as I will more circumstantially reueale
vnto you presently, after a word or two with my fellow prisoner,
for which I craue your fauour.

speeches.speaker: Bull.
prose:
With all my heart, so you can speake Spanish and make
him vnderstand you.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:
You see I am not the Woman you tooke me for: but one
ordain'd for your greater good. If you will giue me my present
demand. I will turne all your disgrace into laughter; make you
of worthier esteeme now at the instant, then euer you were, by
the generall approbation of these, and all that know you beside.
Your Neece to shall be restor'd to your owne liking, and all shall
be as well as you can wish. Otherwise, if you haue a mind to bee
euerlastingly sham'd, by being perpetually laught at, take your
owne course, Ile take mine.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose: I am astonish'd. What is your Demaund?

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:
Whereas your purpose was to make a Whore. Make me
your honest Wife; no more. Bee sodaine in your resolue, all will
be naught else.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:
I am in a mischieuous streight then. Redime to captum.
Thy wit deserues my loue. Ile do't; here's my hand and faith, Ile



do't. Tho^ art mine, and I am thine directly.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose: Then ^earke you sir.

speeches.speaker: Tri
prose:
Sir what will you say, if this Gentlewoman conuert the
Spaniard, turne him true English subiect, and present him to you
with the oaths of Alegiance, & S^premacie in his mouth presently?

speeches.speaker: Bull
prose: I wil say, she ^e^erues ^or euer hereafter to hold her peace.

speeches.speaker: Tra.
prose:
Now bear^ vp sir. Looke confidently, and say, you put on
your Disguise purp^sely to intertaine disguis'd Guests. Come auant
with your Picca de goat, and beginne with the Iustice here.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:
Thou hast made me a M^n for euer, and I will make thee
a Woman directly. Gallants saue you. See here the Metamor.
phosis, that meanes to metamorphose you all. Alas I know you for
all your Disguises, and thought to intertaine you in your k^nd.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
prose: Sir P^ul Squelch!

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:
I^st out of you, my Vsurper, and most Vpstartical
Iustice, whose o^lice is your trade, and Clearke your Prentice, I
will draw a man of litle, or no Moment: yet my frend, and Master
Bulfinch, out of the Chaire of Iustice. ^his my prognosticate
the p^t^ing of my selfe, or many others out of Commission within
these few yeares; though I am no Prophet. Doe I speake English
now? Doe I know you now, or you me?

speeches.speaker: Bull.
prose:
Question ^, we should know one another sir Paul: or
else o^e of vs two were both very ignorant.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:
To proceed in my Metamorphosis. I will change you
most confus'd Roarer, into an accomplisht Knight. And bid you
welcome, noble sir Phillip Lucklesse.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: I like the change well, and thanke you sir.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:
Next sir of you Roarer, or Iieter, or whatsoeuer you are,
I will make a compleat Gentleman, most answerable to you name
Master Tridewell.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose: Very well sir.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:
But out of you Master Doctor, I will pick a certaine
Knane. W^ere is my Neece slrah?

speeches.speaker: Pa.
prose: Which of your N^eces sir?

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:
Haue I so many sir? I meane my only one Constance, find
her me, ^r I will translate you out of an Aesculapian Cocke into a
Newg^e
^ird immediatly.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
Sir if you will Metamorphose me out of a Batch^ lor, into
a Bridegroome, Ile shew you your Neece.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose: This my Neece?

speeches.speaker: Vex.
prose:
O haue I found you Mistris? Sir this is the Gentlewoman
I brought before your worship to day.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose: Hold they peace; art in thy right mind?

speeches.speaker: Vex.
prose:
As I am in my right mind and Midlesex, it is she sir. I
had not matter enough then to lay to her charge; for which I
thanke your worship I kist Newgate. But now I haue sir; she has
lest a Child vpon our Parish, I am sure got by an vnknowne father;
and has beene a loose Liuen, both at Duke Humfreyes, and
most of the winkd it houses about the Towne these foure yeares:
which I can sufficiently proue.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:
Hold thy peace Knaue. Ile put these plums i' thy mouth
else

speeches.speaker: Hold.
prose:
Sir, my Child shall trouble your Parish no longer, here
is a Father, my troth plight Husband, sufficient to keepe it and
me, wilt thou not Duck?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: Duck? my name is Widgi^e, you mistake the man sure.

speeches.speaker: Hold.
prose:
Sure I doe not. This Gentleman, and this Gentlewoman,
and this trusty Seruant of ours are my witnesses, I am your
Wife sir.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
O I am vn^one, quite cast away. Sister helpe mee now
with your Law wit, or I perish for euer.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
This is not to bee endured: cheating, and vile abuse, This
contract can not bee lawfull. One person mistaken for another a
lawfull impediment to be diuore'd for, though they were married.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
I^ might doe well if (as hee con^esses himselfe) he had not
made all too sure, as well within as with^ut.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:
Sir Phillip, while they wrangle out their cause, l^t vs agree:
Find you but the meanes to make her lawfully your Wife,
and here take her with my faithfull promise, of the equall halfe of
any estate presently.

speeches.speaker: Luc.
prose: Sir Paul I thanke you.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
I say this is no lawfull contract: And though we are legally
diuorc'd, yet neither he nor I may lawfully marry, while w^
both liue, hauing beene lawfully married. And till you can disproue
that, sir Ile forbid your Banes good sir Phillip, and lay your
hopes a cooling, frendly Master Tridewell, for your loue in managing
this businesse.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
Lady giue me leaue, if I haue strayn'd a point of friendship,
it was your loue gaue the strenght to my wit. Fit.
^ loue?

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
Your loue indeed Lady. Which (and which Cupid pardon
me for) now, that I see I may enioy, I am not so eagerly taken
with, yet if you will—

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
Sir you cannot enioy me, not he her, lesse you can disproue



the lawfulnesse of our former Mariage.

speeches.speaker: Tri
prose: To cleare that point, doe you know the Minister?

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: Tis not so long since, but I can remember his face.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
Then to continue sir Pauls Metamorphosis? Ile draw him
out of this Doctor. Is not this hee?

speeches.speaker: Fit
prose: It is. But is not hee a lawfull Minister; I would know that.

speeches.speaker: Pate.
prose: To cleare that doubt there lyes my Order of Priesthood.

speeches.speaker: Omnes.
prose: Who, Oliuer!—

speeches.speaker: Pate.
prose:
Euen hee, the Parson Nochurch, and this my Patron, whom
I must beseech together with the whole company, to preserue me
out of the high Commission: for looke you, here is againe your
Licence.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose: Would you doe this Master Tridewell?

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
Faith I foresaw an vnto wardnesse in the Match: which if
you repent the breach of, there's your Licence; and the way to
Church lyes before you.

speeches.speaker: Fit.
prose:
No sir. First get my brother free
of his contract, and then a Licence with your owne name, and
Ile waite on you to Church, as soone as you will.

speeches.speaker: Tri.
prose:
O that's
done already. What are ^ou agreed?

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
Most happily sir, sister
alls well againe. I haue giuen her a hundred pound to relinquish
her right in me. Which afore all these witnesses you doe; doe you
not?

speeches.speaker: Hol.
prose: Yes most freely.

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose:
Well then, I will not forsweare
to marry, But if euer I steale a Wife againe, let her be a
witch, and may I ourn with her for company. Gouernour, thou art
out of countenance, and thou too honest Humfrey, me thinkes.
Come beare vp. I forgiue. Twas your errors, not malice.

speeches.speaker: Ho^.
prose: Sir for my part, ile take my corporall oath—

speeches.speaker: Wid.
prose: It s^ll not need good Humfrey.

speeches.speaker: An.
prose:
And for me sir—wid. Nay, I dare not but beeleeue
th^e before thou speakest Couernour: therefore prithee lets not
talke o^'t our selues, but quietly, and presently beginne our trauels,
that we may heare no body else talke on't.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
prose:
Gentlemen and
L^dies, I
^ee you all at peace^o well, that I wish no further content
to any, except Master Nonsense h^re.

speeches.speaker: Nons.
prose:
Neuer credit me but I
haue had sport en^ugh'o conscience, and if I doe not make a Stage
phyen't, when I come into Cornewall: I protest and vow then say
there was Nonsense in this.

speeches.speaker: Squ.
verse: You ^re all Welcome: And I wish euery Guest
as merry, as our Northern ^asses Feast.
prose:
I am glad you conclude so
^rendly with the rest. All the vnquietnesse will be in the Kitchin
presently If your meat stay for you. Gallants.
I was time to speake. They knock at Dresser already. Will yee in?
